name: Color analysis

card.summary: Seasonal colour analysis: matching clothing and makeup palettes to skin undertone, hair and eyes; popular and low-risk, but little rigorous research backs its specific categories.
card.aka: seasonal color analysis, color draping, 'finding your season'
card.note: Different analysts and apps can assign the same person to different seasons; published validation is sparse.

quick.overview:
Color analysis sorts people into palettes, traditionally the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn and winter, based on skin undertone, hair and eye colour. Followers wear the colours assigned to their season in the belief that these make skin look clearer and the face more harmonious.

The method was popularised in the early 1980s and went viral again on TikTok in the early 2020s. Its categories are widely used but have little peer-reviewed validation.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners hold coloured fabric near the face, usually in daylight, and judge how it affects skin, eyes and overall contrast. Variants add dimensions such as undertone, lightness and chroma, expanding the four seasons to twelve or more sub-seasons.
quick.risks: There is no physical risk. Critics cited in encyclopedia coverage point to subjectivity, oversimplified categories, paid consultations and the encouragement of buying new clothes. Early systems were criticised for centring white clients.

lead: Color analysis, also called seasonal or personal color analysis, is a styling method that advises people which clothing, makeup and hair colours suit them, based on skin, hair and eye colouring. People use it to look clearer-skinned, brighter-eyed and more harmonious by wearing shades matched to their own colouring, which makes it one of the cheapest appearance upgrades discussed in style and looksmaxxing circles, since it requires no procedure and can be tried at home or in a paid session [1][2][7].

Most systems sort people into four seasons (winter, spring, summer, autumn) with sub-variants, usually by undertone (cool blue versus warm yellow), lightness and contrast between hair, skin and eyes [1][2]. The modern consumer version was popularised by consultant Carole Jackson's 1980 book Color Me Beautiful, building on earlier work by Johannes Itten, Robert Dorr, Suzanne Caygill and Bernice Kentner, and it went viral again on TikTok in the early 2020s, with consultants, creators and AI apps offering to find a person's season [1][2][3][7].

Published research is small. A 2021 study at the University of St Andrews found that observers tended to match bluer clothing to fair skin and orange-red clothing to tanned skin, a pattern that fits the idea that skin tone guides flattering colour choice [4]. A 2007 thesis compared three commercial systems and reported inconsistencies in how they used hue, saturation and value [1]. Research on specific colours, such as a meta-analysis of the effect of red on perceived attractiveness, covers adjacent questions rather than seasonal palettes themselves [8].

chain: Assess undertone, depth and contrast of skin, hair and eyes
Choose clothing, makeup and hair shades matched to that palette
Skin looks more even and features more defined next to flattering colours
angle.text: People use their assigned palette to pick shirts, collars, makeup and hair colour that sit well against their complexion. Followers say this reduces a washed-out or sallow look near the face and makes eyes and features stand out, without any procedure or product.

paras: Practitioners assess skin undertone (warm, cool or neutral), value (lightness or depth) and chroma (brightness or muting), together with hair and eye colour [3]. In the classic four-season model, winters are described as suiting rich saturated shades, summers softer muted tones, springs bright warm colours and autumns earthy hues [2]. Sub-seasons used in the viral form include soft, warm, clear, bright, deep and cool variants, such as deep winter, bright spring and soft summer [6][7].

The usual technique is draping: fabric swatches, often on a neutral bib, are held near the face, ideally in daylight because artificial light can shift how colours appear, to see how each shade affects skin and eyes [3][7]. At-home variants include comparing white fabrics or gold versus silver jewellery, vein checks, and camera filters that place the face inside colour wheels [3][7]. Wikipedia notes that many systems treat skin tone as the deciding factor and regard a person's season as fixed over a lifetime, even after tanning [1].

Followers apply the palette to everyday clothing near the face (tops, scarves, collars), to foundation, eyeliner and lipstick shades, to jewellery metals and to hair colour. The stated aim is to look healthier and more vibrant with no change to the face itself [3][7]. Proponents quoted in a 2024 New York Times report say it makes shopping more efficient and getting dressed less overwhelming, comparing it to knowing one's zodiac sign [5]. A creator interviewed by a UK magazine lists glowing skin, wardrobe rebuilding and improved mood among the reported benefits [7]. It is therefore discussed alongside makeup, grooming and wardrobe advice in style-focused appearance communities.

Michel Eugène Chevreul's 1839 work on colour contrast and Albert Munsell's hue, value and chroma system (1905) supplied the vocabulary later used by analysts [1]. Johannes Itten linked personal colouring to the four seasons in his teaching and in his 1961 book The Art of Color [1]. Robert Dorr developed the Color Key System separating cool-undertone and warm-undertone groups, and Suzanne Caygill, who ran a San Francisco salon from 1945, published Color: The Essence of You in 1980 [1][3].

Cheaper colour printing in the 1970s and 1980s enabled mass-market books by Bernice Kentner (Color Me a Season, 1978 or 1979 depending on source) and Carole Jackson [1][6]. Jackson's Color Me Beautiful (1980) became a bestseller, reaching its 31st printing by 1983; the Washington Post reported her company grossed 2.5 million dollars in 1982, and licensed consultants gave rise to the phrase 'have you had your colors done' [2]. In 2000 Kathryn Kalisz introduced the twelve-palette Sci\ART system, and 16-season models are described as emerging in the 2010s [3].

A 2024 New York Times report described the practice as drawing views and exasperation on TikTok. It profiled a Texas former stylist who runs 90-minute in-person sessions at 479 dollars and has a video viewed over 30 million times, a creator who analyses celebrities' seasons, and a beauty creator who travelled from Toronto to Seoul for a consultation [5]. Highsnobiety reported that the #coloranalysis hashtag had passed one billion TikTok views, and that the number of colour analysts in Seoul's Mapo district grew from four to more than twenty after Color Society opened there in April 2020 [6].

Selfie-based apps and AI tools have added to the spread. Grokipedia describes tools reporting roughly 70 to 80 percent classification accuracy against human judgement, and notes that some apps have assigned the same person different seasons [3]. The New York Times piece reports that some experts dismiss crowd-sourced methods such as rainbow filters and chatbots, which it says tend to label almost everyone an autumn [5].

A 2007 University of Huddersfield thesis by Tracy Cassidy compared three personal colour analysis systems and reported inconsistencies: although they claimed to use hue, saturation and value, many palettes relied on two of the three [1]. The 2021 i-Perception study by Perrett and Sprengelmeyer had 96 participants (experiment 1) and 75 (experiment 2) adjust the colour of simulated clothing on photographs of twelve young White women, six fair and six tanned. Observers chose cool hues more often for fair faces (for example 0.58 versus 0.37 in one task) and warmer, more yellow colours for tanned faces (77 percent of participants in experiment 1); experiment 2 replicated the pattern. The authors noted that the faces were all young White women, that testing was online and that hair, eye colour and darker skin tones were not examined [4].

Wikipedia also describes a recent study of lipstick categories used by Japanese Instagram influencers, in which warm and cool categories matched measurable colour traits better than the four-season scheme [1]. Neuroscientist and artist Bevil Conway told the New York Times that the field inflates a small amount of science and that what is flattering is subjective, while accepting colour analysis as a tool [5]. Colour-theory educator Peter Donahue argued in Highsnobiety that the artistic colour wheel behind seasonal systems is not perceptually accurate [6]. Critics also say no standard qualification exists for analysts and fees vary widely [1][5].

A related literature concerns whether specific colours change how a person is rated. A 2018 meta-analysis by Lehmann, Elliot and Calin-Jageman found a small effect of red on men's ratings of women's attractiveness (d = 0.26, high heterogeneity) and a very small effect for women rating men, with signs of possible publication bias; it also found medium effects for manipulated facial redness [8]. These studies test single colours, not seasonal palettes.

The most frequent criticism is that the original systems were built around white clients. Reports note that Jackson's book placed people of colour in the winter category, that Black and East Asian people were assumed to be winters by default in a 1989 documentary clip, and that a creator quoted by the New York Times said early viral content often overlooked people with more melanin [2][5][6]. Some analysts, such as a stylist cited by Highsnobiety, now offer analysis tailored to deeper skin tones [6].

Other concerns raised in coverage are subjectivity and disagreement between analysts (a Reddit survey on one celebrity's season split opinion), prescriptive rules that can feel outdated, paid consultations, and the encouragement to replace wardrobes [1][3][5][6]. Defenders say it can narrow choices and boost confidence [5][6].

No studies found. No clinical trial has tested whether wearing a personally assigned seasonal palette changes perceived attractiveness. Perception studies of skin tone and clothing colour preference exist and are described above [4][8].

lore.intro: Colour analysis is discussed in style and appearance communities as a low-cost way to look more polished, and on social media it has become a trend with its own creators, consultants and disputes over accuracy [5][6][7].

claims.claim: Wearing your season's colours makes skin look clearer and brighter.
claims.believers: Analysts and followers say the right shades reduce a sallow or washed-out look and make eyes and features stand out; one creator said discovering her season made shopping more efficient [5][7].
claims.experts: No trial has tested seasonal palettes directly. A 2021 perception study found observers pick bluer clothing for fair skin and warmer colours for tanned skin, which is consistent with skin tone guiding colour choice [4].

claims.claim: Everyone belongs to one of four (or twelve, or sixteen) seasons that stays fixed for life.
claims.believers: Classic systems treat the season as a permanent feature determined by skin tone, unchanged by tanning [1].
claims.experts: Critics say the categories oversimplify continuous variation in pigmentation, and a 2007 thesis found inconsistent use of hue, saturation and value across three systems [1][3].

claims.claim: An in-person draping session with a trained analyst is the most reliable method.
claims.believers: Adherents quoted in the New York Times consider an in-person assessment the best approach [5].
claims.experts: No standard qualification exists for analysts, and no study has compared accuracy of in-person, filter and AI methods; some apps assign the same person different seasons [1][3].

claims.claim: AI apps and filters can identify your season.
claims.believers: Selfie-based tools and camera filters are popular as free alternatives to consultations [3][7].
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports roughly 70 to 80 percent agreement with human judgement and notes lighting and screen calibration limits; the New York Times reports experts saying chatbots tend to label nearly everyone autumn [3][5].

claims.claim: Seasonal analysis works for all skin tones.
claims.believers: Analysts who specialise in deeper skin tones say the framework can be applied accurately when done carefully [6].
claims.experts: Coverage notes the original systems centred white clients and put people of colour in the winter category; the main perception study tested only young White women's faces [2][4][6].

claims.claim: Wearing red (or other specific colours) makes you more attractive.
claims.believers: Colour-psychology proponents link particular colours to attraction and confidence [1].
claims.experts: A 2018 meta-analysis found a small effect of red on men's ratings of women and a very small one for women rating men, with possible publication bias [8].
